primer.text: From Catalysts you already know that helpers open lower-energy routes through a reaction. This note draws those routes as reaction profiles, adding the peak that particles must clear before any product forms. Reading that peak, and the arrow for the overall change, is the skill this note builds.

lessons.title: Reading reaction profiles
lessons.opening: A reaction profile is the energy level diagram grown a curve: it follows the energy as bonds strain, peak and settle. This lesson names the two features examiners want labelled, the enthalpy arrow and the energy hurdle.
keyPoints: Reaction profiles show the relative energies of reactants and products and how energy changes as the reaction progresses.
The height difference between reactants and products represents the overall enthalpy change.
For an exothermic reaction the enthalpy value is negative and the arrow points downwards.
For an endothermic reaction the enthalpy value is positive and the arrow points upwards.
The climb from reactants up to the peak of the curve marks the energy needed to start reacting.

low.restatement: The profile line starts at the reactants, climbs over a hump and settles at the products. The hump is the energy hurdle for starting, and the height drop or climb from start to finish gives the overall change.
low.analogy: It is like a cross-country run: the race starts and finishes at set heights, but the hardest hill in between decides who can even complete the course.
low.examPointer: Label both the enthalpy change arrow and the activation energy rise when drawing a profile.

medium.restatement: A reaction profile traces energy from reactants over a peak to products, with the reactant-to-product gap giving the overall enthalpy change and the reactant-to-peak rise giving the energy hurdle for starting. Downward overall arrows carry negative values for exothermic reactions and upward arrows positive ones for endothermic.
medium.analogy: A theme-park ride climbs its biggest lift hill before any drops; the lift height is the activation energy and the net height change is the enthalpy change.
medium.examPointer: Mark Ea from reactants to peak and ΔH from reactants to products, with the sign matching the direction.

check.stem: What extra feature does a reaction profile show that a simple energy level diagram does not?

options.text: How the energy changes during the course of the reaction
options.explanation: The curve between the levels is the added information a profile carries.

options.text: The temperature of the reaction mixture
options.explanation: Temperature never appears on energy diagrams.

options.text: The concentration of the reactants
options.explanation: Concentration belongs to rate experiments, not profiles.

options.text: The time taken for the reaction
options.explanation: Profiles show energy against progress, not time.

check.stem: What does the rise from reactants to the peak of the curve represent?

options.text: The activation energy required to start the reaction
options.explanation: That initial climb is the minimum energy particles need to react.

options.text: The overall enthalpy change
options.explanation: The enthalpy change is reactants to products, not to the peak.

options.text: The energy released by the products
options.explanation: Release happens on the way down, not on the initial climb.

options.text: The activation energy of the reverse reaction only
options.explanation: The forward barrier is the one drawn from the reactant level.

check.stem: On an exothermic profile, which way does the enthalpy arrow point and what sign carries?

options.text: Downwards with a negative value
options.explanation: Products sit lower, so the overall arrow descends and ΔH is negative.

options.text: Upwards with a positive value
options.explanation: That is the endothermic profile.

options.text: Downwards with a positive value
options.explanation: A downward arrow with a positive sign contradicts itself.

options.text: Upwards with a negative value
options.explanation: Neither half matches exothermic behaviour.

check.stem: Two reactions share the same enthalpy change but reaction X has a higher peak. What follows?

options.text: X needs more energy to get going, so more heat is needed to start it
options.explanation: A taller barrier means a harder start even when the overall change matches.

options.text: X releases more energy overall
options.explanation: The overall change is stated to be the same.

options.text: X must be endothermic and the other exothermic
options.explanation: Equal enthalpy changes mean both point the same way.

options.text: X has no activation energy
options.explanation: Every reaction has some barrier; X's is simply taller.

check.stem: What is the definition of activation energy?

options.text: The minimum energy that reacting particles must have for a reaction to occur
options.explanation: That threshold is exactly what the profile peak measures.

options.text: The total energy stored in all the bonds of the reactants
options.explanation: Stored energy is not the threshold concept.

options.text: The energy released when products form
options.explanation: Release belongs to the product side of the profile.

options.text: The energy needed to raise the temperature by one degree
options.explanation: That is specific heat capacity.

check.stem: State what the height difference between the reactant and product levels shows on a reaction profile.
check.modelAnswer: The height difference represents the overall enthalpy change of the reaction.

check.stem: State the sign of the enthalpy value and the arrow direction for an exothermic profile.
check.modelAnswer: For an exothermic reaction the enthalpy value is negative and the arrow points downwards.

check.stem: Explain what the climb from the reactant level up to the peak of the curve marks on a reaction profile.
check.modelAnswer: The climb marks the activation energy, the energy needed to start the reaction before the products can form.

check.stem: A profile shows the product level above the reactant level with an upward arrow. State the enthalpy sign and the type of change drawn.
check.modelAnswer: The enthalpy value is positive and the profile shows an endothermic change, because the products end higher than the reactants.

lessons.title: Catalysts drawn onto the profile
lessons.opening: A catalyst redraws the profile with a second, lower hump while the start and finish stay put. This lesson sketches that overlay and explains why the lower hump means a faster reaction.
keyPoints: Catalysts provide the reactants with an alternative pathway of lower activation energy.
A lower peak means a greater proportion of molecules have sufficient energy for an effective collision.
The catalysed reaction finishes faster than the same reaction without the catalyst.
The reactant and product levels on the profile are unchanged by adding a catalyst.
Reactions with low activation energy occur readily because little energy is needed to begin.

low.restatement: Draw the same start and finish, then add a smaller hump labelled as the catalysed route. More particles can clear the smaller hump, so the catalysed reaction runs faster even though the overall change is identical.
low.analogy: Two paths over the same hill: the tunnel route needs far less climbing, so more hikers finish per hour.
low.examPointer: Show both humps on one diagram and label the lower one as the catalysed pathway.

medium.restatement: The catalysed profile keeps the original reactant and product levels but offers a lower peak, so a greater proportion of molecules can achieve an effective collision. The catalysed reaction therefore completes faster while the overall enthalpy change stays exactly as before.
medium.analogy: Adding a chairlift does not move the mountain top, but far more skiers reach it each hour; the mountain is the reaction, the lift is the catalyst.
medium.examPointer: State that the peak drops, not the levels, and link the drop to a greater proportion of effective collisions.

check.stem: How does a catalyst appear on a reaction profile?

options.text: As a second curve with a lower peak between the same reactant and product levels
options.explanation: The alternative pathway is drawn lower while the endpoints stay fixed.

options.text: As a deeper valley below the reactant level
options.explanation: The route still climbs to a peak; it is just a smaller one.

options.text: As a new product level lower than before
options.explanation: Product levels are unchanged by catalysis.

options.text: As a vertical line at the start
options.explanation: Catalysts change the pathway shape, not the axes.

check.stem: Why does lowering the peak increase the rate?

options.text: A greater proportion of molecules now have sufficient energy for an effective collision
options.explanation: The smaller hurdle converts average collisions into successful ones.

options.text: Because the molecules themselves become more energetic
options.explanation: Molecule energies are unchanged; the requirement drops.

options.text: Because the products are more stable
options.explanation: Product stability is identical with or without the catalyst.

options.text: Because the reactant level falls
options.explanation: The reactant level never moves.

check.stem: What happens to the overall enthalpy change when a catalyst is added?

options.text: It is unchanged, because the start and finish levels are the same
options.explanation: Catalysts alter the route, never the endpoints.

options.text: It becomes more negative
options.explanation: The drop between levels is fixed.

options.text: It becomes positive
options.explanation: The direction of the overall change is untouched.

options.text: It halves, because the barrier fell
options.explanation: Barrier and overall change are different quantities.

check.stem: A reaction occurs readily at room temperature. What does its profile look like?

options.text: It has a low activation peak, so little energy is needed to begin
options.explanation: Ready reactions correspond to small barriers.

options.text: It has no peak at all
options.explanation: Every reaction has some barrier to clear.

options.text: It has a very high peak
options.explanation: A high peak would make the reaction reluctant, not ready.

options.text: Its product level sits above its reactant level
options.explanation: Readiness says nothing about the sign of the change.

check.stem: The activation energy for a particular reaction is described as what kind of quantity?

options.text: A fixed value for that reaction, unchanged by how fast the reaction is run
options.explanation: The barrier is a property of the reaction and its pathway.

options.text: A value that grows as the reaction proceeds
options.explanation: The barrier is set by the pathway, not by progress.

options.text: A value that depends on the amount of product formed
options.explanation: Yield does not set the barrier.

options.text: A value that changes with the colour of the mixture
options.explanation: Colour has no bearing on the barrier.

check.stem: State what catalysts provide to the reactants on an energy profile.
check.modelAnswer: Catalysts provide the reactants with an alternative pathway of lower activation energy.

check.stem: State how the catalysed and uncatalysed runs differ in the time they take.
check.modelAnswer: The catalysed reaction finishes faster than the same reaction without the catalyst.

check.stem: Explain why lowering the peak of the profile means more molecules can react successfully.
check.modelAnswer: A lower peak means a greater proportion of molecules carries the energy needed for an effective collision, so more collisions succeed.

check.stem: After a catalyst is added to a reaction, a second profile is drawn on the same axes. State what stays identical between the two profiles.
check.modelAnswer: The reactant and product levels stay unchanged by adding the catalyst; only the peak height falls.

glossary.definition: A diagram showing how energy changes as a reaction progresses, including the activation peak.
The minimum energy that reacting particles must have for a reaction to occur.
The energy difference between reactants and products, drawn as the arrow between the levels.
A collision with enough energy to form products, made more likely by a lower peak.
The lower-energy route through a reaction provided by a catalyst.

workedExample.prompt: a) Describe how a reaction profile shows the activation energy and the overall enthalpy change for an exothermic reaction. b) Explain how a catalyst appears on a reaction profile and why it increases the rate. c) What happens to the enthalpy change when a catalyst is added?
steps: a) The curve starts at the reactant level, climbs to a peak and settles at the product level below the reactants: the initial rise from reactants to the peak is the activation energy Ea, and the drop from reactants to products is the overall enthalpy change, which is negative for an exothermic reaction (a downwards arrow).
b) The catalyst provides an alternative pathway with a lower peak: a greater proportion of molecules then have sufficient energy for an effective collision, so the rate increases.
c) The enthalpy change is unchanged — the reactant and product levels stay exactly where they were; only the peak is lowered.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Reactants-to-peak = Ea; reactants-to-products drop = ΔH (negative, exothermic). b) A lower catalysed peak means more effective collisions, so faster. c) Unchanged.
